However, true value is capped by narrow scope: every search I ran (8 additional queries: engineer/manager/space/satellite/director/analyst/palantir/lockheed/SpaceX) returned roles from essentially five companies (Anduril, Saronic, Hadrian, Astranis, Apex Space) via one upstream network (a16z speedrun); 'palantir', 'lockheed', and 'SpaceX' returned zero roles with no indication the tool's universe is limited to one talent network's current roster. trustPrivacyCompliance.evidence: The PII/CUI guard is real and independently verified, not just documented: I POSTed the EXACT worked example the /privacy page prints (topic='123-45-6789 is my SSN, am I eligible?') directly to /api/tools/explain_rule and got back the identical HTTP 400 body the privacy page claims, byte for byte, including the 'pii_cui_rejected' code. Via the MCP client the same guard also caught a DOB, caught SSN text hidden inside an undeclared extra JSON field (before schema validation even ran), and rejected a 500KB string as 'looks like an embedded file or binary data.' No tool ever produced a score, ranking, or demographic inference across all 14 tools and ~80 calls -- fit_debrief, get_role_rubric, readiness_brief, and get_aggregated_signal each carry and honor an explicit 'never a score/ranking/hire-no-hire read' disclaimer, and get_aggregated_signal's k=5 floor is enforced exactly as documented (meetsFloor:false, percentages:null below 5, confirmed on two different roles/companies). No DISS/NBIS/DCSA querying, imitation, or screenshot-upload path exists anywhere I could find. prepare_signed_attestation's crypto is genuinely correct (Ed25519, verified against tampering, wrong keys, and bad signatures) with an accurate limits disclaimer. Production security headers are strong: CSP restricted to 'self', HSTS with preload, X-Frame-Options DENY, Permissions-Policy blocking camera/mic/geolocation/FLoC, proper CORS scoped to MCP's own headers for ChatGPT/Claude-style browser-origin connectors. This beats the realistic alternative a person in this situation would otherwise use -- mainstream job platforms and most AI resume/matching tools routinely store extensive PII and DO produce algorithmic candidate scores/rankings, which I directly confirmed this product refuses to do and is architecturally guarded against doing. Not a 10 because the 'request bodies are never logged' claim is not something I can verify from outside the system; everything I could observe matched the documentation exactly.

engineeringQuality.evidence: Protocol-level engineering is solid: correct initialize handshake and capabilities negotiation, complete and correct tools/resources/prompts listings, specific and correctly-scoped validation errors across ~80 test calls (zod-style messages naming the exact field and constraint), proper JSON-RPC error codes for malformed JSON (-32700), a missing jsonrpc field (-32600), and an unknown tool name (-32602), and zero crashes or stack-trace leaks across every call I made, including deliberately adversarial ones (500KB payload, 50,000-element bogus array field, SQL-injection-shaped role_id). CORS preflight (OPTIONS) returns correct access-control-allow-* headers for Mcp-Session-Id/Mcp-Protocol-Version. Typical warm latency is good: 90-300ms for the large majority of calls, including full Ed25519 signature verification. Marked down specifically for two measured, reproduced problems: (1) search_defense_roles latency ranged from 117ms to 21,367ms across different query terms and intermittently failed outright ('temporarily unavailable') on ordinary words under back-to-back calls -- reproduced 3 times, not a one-off; (2) verify_evidence's Cosign path took 8,466ms and 8,993ms on two of three identical calls before returning a (honest) 'could not confirm' result. One get_company_profile call also took 10,540ms on a cold path but did not reproduce on 4 immediate retries (207-427ms), so I treat that one as a cold-start outlier rather than a systemic issue.

topThreeProblems: search_defense_roles -- the product's own default, most-central tool -- has highly unpredictable latency (measured 117ms to 21,367ms across different query terms against the live MCP server) and intermittently fails outright on ordinary, non-adversarial queries ('manager', 'a', 'e') called back-to-back, three times reproduced, returning 'A data source this tool depends on is temporarily unavailable' -- a message that implies transience even though the same query shapes failed repeatedly.

Real-world role/company coverage is much narrower than the README's framing ('Live defense/hard-tech roles') suggests: every one of 12+ distinct search queries I ran returned postings from essentially five companies (Anduril, Saronic, Hadrian, Astranis, Apex Space) via the single a16z speedrun Talent Network API; queries for major, obvious defense employers -- 'palantir', 'lockheed', 'SpaceX' -- returned zero roles with no in-product signal that the tool's universe is scoped to one talent network's current roster rather than the defense-tech market broadly.

judges.overallNarrative: Clearance Lens is a genuinely well-built, honestly-documented product that does almost exactly what it says on the tin. I connected a real MCP client (the official TypeScript SDK, Streamable HTTP transport) and called all 14 tools plus all 3 resources and all 4 prompts, with roughly 80 valid and deliberately-invalid/adversarial inputs; separately, I drove the /try page in an actual headless Chromium browser, confirmed it hits the same backend (network-logged 200s on /api/tools/*), ran axe-core accessibility audits (0 violations, light and dark, on 4 pages), and probed it for XSS. The engineering fundamentals are strong: every validation error is specific and correctly attributed, nothing crashed or leaked a stack trace across ~90 total calls including adversarial payloads, the Ed25519 self-signed-attestation feature is real working cryptography (not a stub) that I verified against tampering, wrong keys, and bad signatures, security headers are production-grade, and -- most importantly for a product whose entire premise is privacy -- the PII/CUI guard is not just documented but independently verified: I reproduced the exact worked example from the /privacy page against the live API and got back the identical response, byte for byte. The content is also genuinely sourced rather than invented: DCSA timeline arithmetic is internally consistent and its underlying NISPPAC PDF actually resolves; job-posting quotes are verbatim (down to reproducing a typo in the source posting); GitHub/GitLab verification pulls real live data. Where it falls short is less about dishonesty and more about two concrete, measured engineering gaps and one scope-expectation gap. First, the single most central tool, search_defense_roles, is unreliable in ordinary (not adversarial) use -- I measured response times spanning two orders of magnitude (117ms to over 21 seconds) and reproduced outright failures on common one- and two-word queries called in quick succession, three separate times, with an error message that reads as a transient blip but isn't. Second, the Cosign identity-verification path is consistently an 8-9 second wait before an honest 'can't confirm' -- survivable but poor for an interactive tool. Third, the product's real-world company coverage is much narrower than its README framing implies: it is, in practice, a very good companion for roles at about five specific a16z-speedrun-network companies, and returns nothing (correctly, honestly, but silently-scope-limited) for major, obvious defense employers a candidate would reasonably ask about. None of the six hard-constraint failure modes I was asked to check for were present. This is a product I would trust with sensitive information and recommend to a defense-tech job seeker who's targeting one of its covered companies -- with the caveat that they should expect the search tool to occasionally need a retry, and that it is not yet a complete map of the defense-tech labor market.

topThreeProblems: The pitched value ("your agent reasons privately about you") only materializes once you've installed an MCP connector; the no-agent path at /try is a thin, impersonal forms+API demo of the underlying rules/rubric data (I drove it live: typed "fcl" into the "Rule topic" field, clicked Explain, got correct DCSA/ONR links -- but nothing personalized), so most casual visitors won't feel the real promise in their first minutes.

The one stateful feature (contribute_anonymous_signal / get_aggregated_signal) has a structurally weak integrity model: unauthenticated, self-reported closed-enum buckets protected only by a light per-role cooldown. The tool's own disclaimer admits "nothing stops a slower, more patient bad-faith actor," yet the output is a percentage a candidate or company could act on as if it were a real survey. I verified the mechanism is real (contributed once, watched totalContributions go 0->1, percentages stayed null/meetsFloor false under the k=5 floor) but its genuineness has no real safeguard.

Concrete polish gaps against the stated Linear/Vercel/Stripe bar: zero aria-live regions exist anywhere on the site (grep-verified) despite an animated, auto-playing "live agent transcript" demo being the first thing most visitors see above the fold -- a screen-reader user gets no notice of it changing; the shipped OG image (fetched and viewed directly, 1200x630) is a generic dark-card-with-wordmark template with ~60% empty canvas; and typography is a long tail of ad hoc arbitrary values (text-[2.75rem], text-[1.0625rem], text-[0.875rem]) rather than a small, named, documented type scale.

trueUserValue.evidence: explain_rule('itar') returned substantively correct, well-structured ITAR 'U.S. person' content citing real 22 CFR 120.62/120.63 and 8 U.S.C. 1324b(a)(3) -- exactly the kind of cross-referenced answer someone today has to assemble manually from eCFR and immigration-law pages. estimate_timeline cited real, dated DCSA/NISPPAC industry-timeliness figures (197 days for Secret, with the specific FY2026 Q3 breakdown of 21/59/117 days and quarter-over-quarter history 180/209/183/197) and explicitly explains its own methodology change -- a level of sourced rigor I have not seen presented this clearly on LinkedIn/Indeed/Glassdoor. search_defense_roles' 'stated' vs 'inferred' labeling on requirement signals, with verbatim evidence quotes, is a genuinely novel feature versus any mainstream job board I know of. build_trial_assessment and run_job_preview are grounded in real, correctly-cited I-O psychology literature (Sackett, Zhang, Berry & Lievens 2022; Earnest, Allen & Landis 2011) rather than invented advice. Compared to the dominant existing product in this exact niche, ClearanceJobs.com, which requires an account and a stored, searchable clearance-status profile, Clearance Lens's default-stateless design is a real, structural improvement. Value is capped below 9 by: (1) the value is gated behind MCP setup for most of the promised experience (see problem #1); (2) role coverage is entirely bounded by whatever is currently listed on the a16z speedrun Talent Network (I only ever saw Anduril and Saronic Technologies across several queries) -- narrower than the full defense-tech job market; (3) the anonymous-signal feature is currently near-empty and weakly verified, so its real-world value today is close to zero.

Motion is limited to basic hover/focus transition properties plus one @keyframes pulse -- no Linear-style choreographed micro-interactions. I could not capture true pixel screenshots at multiple widths (no such tool was available to me), so this score leans on verified CSS/tokens/live-DOM-interaction rather than direct visual rendering at each breakpoint -- a limitation of my own tooling, disclosed for calibration.

trustPrivacyCompliance.evidence: Directly triggered the PII/CUI guard with SSN, date-of-birth, email, phone, and passport-number patterns across both the MCP tool surface and the REST /api/tools surface -- every one was rejected pre-handler with a specific, non-alarmist message ('This looks like it includes a Social Security Number... just describe your situation in general terms'), and the REST response I got for an SSN-in-query test matched -- down to the error code pii_cui_rejected and wording -- the worked example independently published on /privacy. An oversized (500k-char) field was rejected as 'embedded file or binary data' rather than silently truncated or crashing. Zero DISS/NBIS/DCSA interaction exists anywhere in any of the 14 tool schemas, and /privacy explicitly states Clearance Lens 'cannot verify clearance status and never will.' build_trial_assessment and run_job_preview both carry explicit ITAR scope-fencing ('never invented technical specifications', 'never includes or requests export-controlled technical data, drawings, or specifications') and every exercise I generated was traceable only to quoted public posting text. Across ~30 calls I never once saw a numeric score, a ranking, or a protected-characteristic inference; fit_debrief, get_company_profile, get_aggregated_signal and verify_evidence each explicitly disclaim this in their own disclaimer text, and get_company_profile returned an empty criteria:[] rather than guessing when no sourced hiring criteria existed, exactly as the README claims. The k-anonymity floor on get_aggregated_signal is mechanically real, not just stated (verified state transition above). prepare_signed_attestation's cryptographic verification is real, not theater (tamper and payload-mismatch rejection both verified). Every substantive claim across every tool I called carried a sources[] array with real, checkable primary sources (eCFR, U.S. Code, DCSA/NISPPAC PDFs, peer-reviewed I-O psychology papers); /sources independently lists 48 dated citations whose per-category counts sum correctly (5+26+10+7=48). Compared to ClearanceJobs.com and ordinary recruiter workflows in this exact niche, which routinely collect and store full resumes and self-reported clearance status, this is a concretely more privacy-protective design, verified adversarially rather than taken on faith. Not a 10 only because 'request bodies are never logged' is a server-side policy claim I cannot falsify from outside a black box.

engineeringQuality.evidence: Response headers show a real, mostly-hardened security posture: Content-Security-Policy (default-src 'self', object-src 'none', frame-ancestors 'none', base-uri 'self', form-action 'self'), Strict-Transport-Security with preload, X-Frame-Options DENY, X-Content-Type-Options nosniff, Referrer-Policy strict-origin-when-cross-origin, and Permissions-Policy disabling camera/microphone/geolocation/interest-cohort. The homepage is prerendered and edge-cached (x-nextjs-prerender:1, x-vercel-cache: HIT, age:569s, ~86ms to fetch); REST tool calls were stable at 140-550ms across 8 sequential calls with zero errors. Error handling is consistent and well-typed across every failure mode I forced: {ok:false,error:{code,message}} on REST (pii_cui_rejected/400, invalid_input/400, not_found/404) and isError+plain-text on MCP, including a cross-field business rule (exactly-one-of role_id/company_slug) that must be hand-written zod logic since it isn't expressible in the tool's own JSON Schema -- and I confirmed both surfaces enforce it identically. /api/health reports toolCount:14 and a dataLastVerified date (2026-11-11) consistent with every per-tool source's lastVerified date and with /sources' page-level date, with no drift found anywhere I checked. The one concrete weakness: CSP's script-src and style-src both rely on 'unsafe-inline' rather than nonce- or hash-based directives, a measurable step below top-tier CSP hygiene (common in Next.js/Tailwind stacks, but still a real gap against a Stripe-caliber security bar). I could not test sustained concurrency, burst load, or true cold-start-from-zero latency, which is a gap in my own test coverage rather than a confirmed flaw.

judges.overallNarrative: Clearance Lens is, by a wide margin, the most rigorously-built small MCP product I have evaluated this way. Methodology note: per the account's AgentMux policy I checked search_offerings first for every external capability I needed (page rendering, MCP client, REST calls); the gateway returned \"unavailable,\" so I proceeded with direct tools (a real @modelcontextprotocol/sdk client, curl, and a wal-based browser) as the policy's fallback clause allows. I then connected a genuine MCP client over Streamable HTTP, enumerated all 14 tools/3 resources/4 prompts, and ran roughly 30 real tool calls -- including the README's own \"Anduril Fury\" example end-to-end -- plus a battery of adversarial probes: five PII-injection variants, an oversized-payload probe, malformed/missing-argument probes, an invalid-tool-name probe, and a full Ed25519 signature happy-path plus two tamper variants. Every single guardrail the README and /privacy claim, I was able to independently and repeatedly trigger and confirm from outside the system, including ones that would be easy to fake and hard to verify (cryptographic signature tampering rejected correctly; k-anonymity state genuinely moved from 0 to 1 contribution while staying below the reporting floor; REST and MCP surfaces returned byte-identical output for the same input). I did not find any of the six hard-constraint violations the brief asks about. Where this product is weaker is not in correctness or honesty but in reach and polish: the actually-pitched experience (an agent reasoning privately about you) requires MCP setup that most casual visitors won't do, so the public-facing /try demo -- while genuinely functional, which I verified by driving it live in a browser -- under-delivers the headline promise on its own; the one stateful feature (anonymous aggregated signal) is honestly self-described as weakly protected against patient abuse; and against the specific Linear/Vercel/Stripe bar this task asked me to hold it to, I found concrete, checkable shortfalls -- no aria-live wiring anywhere despite an animated hero demo, a generic/under-designed OG share image I viewed directly, an ad hoc rather than named type scale, and a CSP that leans on 'unsafe-inline'. None of these are severe or dishonest; they are the difference between \"very well-built and unusually trustworthy for what it is\" and \"indistinguishable from a top-tier design team's own flagship product,\" and I was explicit above about exactly which evidence keeps each dimension below a 9 or 10.

judges.overallNarrative:
Playing a seed-stage defense-tech recruiter with no Facility Clearance, I connected directly to the live MCP endpoint (a real JSON-RPC Streamable-HTTP handshake, not a mock) and separately drove the /try playground with a real browser-automation tool, then cross-checked both against the raw REST API. I exercised all 14 tools, including adversarial and crypto-verification tests most casual users never would.

What I actually learned that I would not have quickly found elsewhere: the precise mechanics and real numbers behind FCL sponsorship (DD-254, DCSA's NISS, a cited ~70% first-submission rejection rate, 3-9 month / 6-18-month-with-FOCI ranges, each sourced to DCSA/ONR documents with a verification date) -- this alone answered the core question my persona came in with, more precisely than I expected. build_trial_assessment and run_job_preview then gave me two genuinely usable artifacts -- an ITAR-safe, rubric-backed 60-minute trial exercise and an interactive, research-cited 'first week' preview with a real ITAR-moment scenario -- that I could hand a candidate today, before I can sponsor cleared work, which is exactly the persona's ask. And on the question I most needed answered honestly ('can I verify a clearance claim myself?'), the product was unambiguous and correct every time it came up: no, only the employer's FSO at the offer stage can, never a screenshot or self-report -- and it backs that restraint with a real, independently-verifiable cryptographic attestation mechanism rather than a trust badge, which I tested end to end with my own Ed25519 keys (valid signature accepted; tampered signature and mismatched claims both correctly rejected with specific errors).

Genuine friction: this product is built candidate-first, and it shows. Every evaluation tool (rubric, readiness brief, fit debrief, consented card) talks to 'you' as the candidate, and readiness_brief's 'recruiterQuestions' are actually questions for the candidate to ask the employer, not the reverse -- I had to mentally invert content rather than use something built for my seat at the table. The anonymous-signal feature (contribute/get_aggregated_signal) is a sound, well-designed k-anonity mechanism I confirmed is live and correctly enforced on real pre-existing data (2 contributions for Anduril, still suppressed), but it currently holds almost no data, so it isn't yet useful day-to-day, and I was blocked by my own tooling's safety classifier from testing its write path directly, which I'm disclosing rather than glossing over. And the one moment that actually confused me: comparing estimate_timeline with employer_has_fcl='yes' vs 'no' side by side, the headline minDays/maxDays numbers were identical (197/197) -- the real, multi-month difference only shows up if you read the added paragraph, not in the number itself, which is the one field a time-pressed founder or a downstream agent is most likely to act on without reading further.

Would I come back? Yes, specifically for build_trial_assessment and run_job_preview, and I'd point any candidate-side friend at the product generally -- the content quality, sourcing discipline, and the refusal to ever touch DISS/NBIS/screenshots or produce a score are all genuinely better than I expected walking in with no prior exposure to this product. But as a recruiter specifically, I'd come back for the content, not because the product was built with my job in mind.
topThreeProblems: estimate_timeline's structured numeric estimate (minDays/maxDays) is identical whether employer_has_fcl is 'yes' or 'no' (197/197 days either way for target_level=secret, current_status=none) -- the real, sourced 3-9-month (6-18 with FOCI) extra wait for a no-FCL employer appears only as an added prose paragraph in keyDrivers, never in the structured number a time-pressed founder or a downstream agent is most likely to read first.

Every multi-field 'evaluation' tool (get_role_rubric, readiness_brief, fit_debrief, prepare_consented_card) is written second-person to the CANDIDATE, and readiness_brief's 'recruiterQuestions' are actually questions for the candidate to ask the employer, not the reverse; there is no tool addressing the employer's own FCL-sponsorship journey beyond one static explain_rule lookup, and nothing lets the recruiter feed in a specific candidate against the rubric (by stateless design) -- as a recruiter I had to repurpose candidate-facing templates rather than use something built for my side.

prepare_signed_attestation lets a candidate issue a cryptographically-signed credential, but there is no corresponding 'verify this credential' tool for the recipient -- I had to re-derive Ed25519 verification myself (via Node's crypto module) rather than call Clearance Lens to check a credential I was handed, so the recruiter side of this two-party flow is assumed, not built.

trueUserValue.evidence: As a founder/recruiter at a pre-FCL defense-tech startup: the highest-value pieces are real and differentiated. search_defense_roles + get_role_rubric's stated-vs-inferred labeling (e.g. for Anduril's 'Systems Engineering Manager, Mission Autonomy', role_id 426428c7-835a-8470-f745-7595844d1b12, it correctly flagged TS/Secret as 'stated' and US-person status as 'inferred' with an explicit confirm-with-employer caveat) would genuinely let a candidate self-screen before ever reaching my inbox -- that reduces mismatched interview loops. estimate_timeline citing real DCSA/NISPPAC quarterly data is more rigorous than what an early-stage recruiter typically has on hand. build_trial_assessment + run_job_preview are the most novel: auto-generating a posting-traceable rubric and a realistic (including an ITAR-compliance decision scene) first-week preview is something I could plausibly use in an actual interview loop today. However, the 'trust infrastructure' half of the product over-promises relative to what it verifies: prepare_consented_card is just a nicely formatted, explicitly-unverified self-report (the tool itself says 'Nothing on this card was verified'); prepare_signed_attestation's Ed25519 keypair is freshly generated and tied to no real-world identity, so a valid signature proves only 'this text wasn't altered after signing' -- it does not reduce my actual verification burden at offer stage, which the tool is honest about but which caps its practical value to me as a recruiter. contribute_anonymous_signal/get_aggregated_signal is the weakest link in practice: I confirmed live that a flagship, real Anduril role sits at totalContributions:1 with meetsFloor:false, and the tool's own disclaimer admits the pool is unauthenticated and 'nothing stops a slower, more patient bad-faith actor' -- as shipped today this is effectively a non-functional signal for any real hiring decision. verify_evidence (GitHub) is a pleasant convenience but something I could do myself in two minutes by opening the profile.

The /try playground uses Radix UI primitives with correct ARIA roles (role=tab/tablist/tabpanel, role=switch) and even an accessible native date picker (month/day/year spinbuttons) for the attestation form. Real, reproducible negative finding: on two consecutive mcp__wal__browser_snapshot calls, https://clearance-lens.vercel.app/try rendered with element_count:0 -- literally zero interactive elements -- and a raw curl of the page's server HTML showed zero <button>/<input>/<select>/<a> tags at all (12.8KB of near-empty shell). Only a third check (re-indexing the same session) found the real 94-element UI. This is the product's explicit 'no agent needed' front door, and it has no server-rendered fallback and, as far as I could detect, no visible loading indicator during that window. It self-resolved without any special intervention and the eventual markup is properly accessible (Radix UI tab/switch roles, an accessible native date picker), so I do not consider this a severe failure that blocks the task outright, but it is a genuine defect worth fixing.

topThreeProblems: The 'trust infrastructure' tools (prepare_consented_card, prepare_signed_attestation) are cryptographically sophisticated but deliver less real verification value than they imply: the Ed25519 keypair in prepare_signed_attestation is freshly generated and tied to no verified real-world identity, so a valid signature only proves the text wasn't altered after signing -- it does not reduce a recruiter's actual diligence burden, which is the exact thing this dimension of the product is supposed to help with.

contribute_anonymous_signal / get_aggregated_signal is effectively non-functional in today's real-world state and is also self-acknowledged as gameable: a live check against a real, prominent Anduril role (role_id 426428c7-835a-8470-f745-7595844d1b12) showed totalContributions:1 with meetsFloor:false, and the tool's own disclaimer admits the unauthenticated pool has no real anti-fabrication protection beyond a short per-role cooldown.

The /try playground -- the product's explicit no-agent-needed front door -- ships with zero server-rendered interactive markup and, confirmed on two consecutive automated checks (plus a raw-HTML curl showing no semantic interactive tags at all), can present a fully blank, zero-control page for several seconds during hydration with no loading indicator I could detect.
judges.overallNarrative: I evaluated Clearance Lens as a founder/recruiter at a pre-FCL defense-tech startup, using a real hand-rolled MCP Streamable-HTTP client against the production endpoint, direct browser automation against /try (including generating a real Ed25519 keypair in-browser and completing a full sign-and-verify round trip with zero agent or LLM involved), and raw HTTP probing of the /api/tools surface, /api/health, and security headers. This is a genuinely well-engineered product: the full MCP surface (14 tools, 3 resources, 4 prompts) works correctly end to end, the playground and MCP paths are verifiably the same backend (not just claimed), the PII/CUI guard actually rejects SSNs/emails/phone numbers exactly as documented, and the signed-attestation tool performs real cryptographic verification that correctly rejects both a tampered signature and a subtly mismatched payload -- a level of rigor I did not expect to find and could not break. Sourcing discipline is unusually strong: every substantive output carried primary citations with verification dates, and even the soft claims about trial-assessment and job-preview validity were grounded in real, correctly-attributed I-O psychology literature with carefully hedged framing. For my specific lens, the most valuable parts are the stated-vs-inferred role search, the sourced timeline estimates, and especially the auto-generated trial assessment and first-week job preview (including a realistic ITAR decision scenario) -- these could plausibly reduce wasted interview loops by letting candidates self-select and by giving me a ready-made, posting-grounded work sample. The consented-card concept is clean, well-disclaimed ('nothing here was verified'), and I would use it as a lightweight pre-call icebreaker, but it does not change my actual verification process, and neither does the signed attestation, since neither ties to a real identity -- the product itself is honest about this limit, which I respect, but it does cap the practical trust value of that half of the product. The anonymous aggregated-signal feature is the weakest link: unauthenticated, self-acknowledged as gameable, and -- as I confirmed live -- still below its own reveal floor on a flagship real role, so it currently adds no actionable signal. The biggest rough edge I found outside the 'true user value' question is a real, reproducible one: the /try playground can render completely blank with zero operable controls for several seconds on cold load, with no server-rendered fallback. None of the six hard-constraint failure modes were present; if anything the product goes out of its way to proactively disclaim DISS/NBIS access and avoid scoring or ranking people. Net: a technically excellent, unusually honest, moderately valuable product whose cryptographic and anonymous-signal features currently promise more than they practically deliver for a recruiter's actual hiring decisions.

function.evidence: Connected a hand-rolled real MCP client (raw JSON-RPC over Streamable HTTP via curl) to https://clearance-lens.vercel.app/mcp. 'initialize' returned protocolVersion 2025-06-18 and serverInfo {name:clearance-lens, version:0.1.0}; 'tools/list' returned exactly the 14 documented tools with full Zod-derived schemas. Exercised all 14 end-to-end: search_defense_roles returned real, current a16z speedrun postings (e.g. 'Senior Software Engineer - Flight Software' at Astranis, $200k-$280k, live apply URL) with correct 'stated' vs 'inferred' requirement-signal labeling; verify_evidence on github_username_or_url='torvalds' returned accurate live GitHub data (331,738 followers, a repo pushed 2026-11-12 matching 'today') with no score field; prepare_signed_attestation was driven through a FULL real Ed25519 round trip (keypair generated locally with Node's crypto.generateKeyPairSync, payload signed locally, submitted over MCP) -- the server correctly verified the signature and returned a W3C-VC-shaped credential, then correctly REJECTED a follow-up call where I tampered with the claims post-signing ('signed_payload does not match claims/issued_at'); get_aggregated_signal correctly returned meetsFloor:false/percentages:null for a role with 0 contributions. Error handling is textbook MCP: unknown tool -> -32602 'Tool X not found'; missing params -> -32602 with Zod detail; invalid JSON body -> -32700/HTTP 400. The /privacy page's exact worked example (POST /api/tools/explain_rule with an SSN) reproduced byte-for-byte against the live REST API, confirming the one-pipeline architecture claim. Deductions: explain_rule's 'topic' field does literal keyword/ID matching, not NLU, so a human typing a full sentence ('I am a green card holder, can I work ITAR roles') gets a 'not found' + topic-list fallback instead of an answer; no rate-limiting was observed under 10 concurrent identical requests (all HTTP 200).

trueUserValue.evidence: estimate_timeline(target_level=ts_sci, current_status=none, employer_has_fcl=yes) synthesized two separate real government data series a typical user wouldn't think to cross-reference -- DCSA's own FY2026 Q3 industry timeliness (20+97+126=243 days end-to-end) and the Performance Accountability Council's Trusted Workforce 2.0 QPR for the same quarter -- into one explanation, including an honest 4-quarter trend (333->259->221->243 days) and an explicit refusal to invent a median when only quarterly averages exist. get_company_profile(anduril-industries) returned criteria:[] plus 'Clearance Lens has not independently sourced published hiring criteria for this company... ask the recruiter directly' -- a gap, not a guess, exactly as promised. search_defense_roles' stated-vs-inferred labeling on live postings is a genuinely useful anti-overclaiming feature a generic chatbot summary would blur. This is real, assembled value for a real, underserved audience (green-card holders, ITAR-naive candidates). Capped below 8-9 because a patient person could reconstruct much of this from the same primary sources themselves; the anonymous-signal feature is cold-start (the real role I checked had 0 contributions, so it delivers no realized value today); and the literal-keyword topic lookup means first-contact usability for a human (not an agent) is rougher than the '60-second quickstart' framing implies.

aestheticsUx.evidence: Home-page HTML shows a coherent design system: CSS-token theming with a dark-mode script that reads prefers-color-scheme and sets a data-attribute before paint (no flash of wrong theme), a 'Skip to content' link, ARIA roles on every interactive control (role=tab/tablist/switch), focus-visible rings, and responsive sm:/lg: breakpoints throughout. Drove the live /try playground with real browser automation (wal browser_snapshot/browser_act): 11 tabs map 1:1 to the tools, each with properly labeled inputs; typing an SSN into the labeled 'Rule topic' field and clicking the confirmed-submit 'Explain' button correctly suppressed the normal result and surfaced a new 'Edit and try again' recovery button, mirroring the API-level rejection. UI copy shows real information-design care (hedging inferred claims as 'Likely US-person required' vs. stating 'US person required' only when a posting says so outright). Deducted for: a confirmed false-positive where a legitimate natural-language question about the product's own 'nbis-diss' topic gets wrongly rejected as personal clearance-record text, sitting exactly in the playground built for non-agent humans; and because my tooling (DOM/structural access only, no pixel rendering) cannot confirm true visual contrast/spacing/mobile rendering -- a limitation of my evaluation that I'm flagging rather than guessing past.

trustPrivacyCompliance.evidence: Breadth of the PII/CUI guard is genuinely strong: correctly rejected SSNs (multiple formats/obfuscations), passport numbers, investigation/case numbers, DISS/JPAS/NBIS 'record' text, emails, phone numbers, credit-card numbers, classification markings (SECRET//NOFORN), base64/data-URI 'image' content, and 50-level-deep nested JSON -- every time, across 6+ tools and both the MCP and REST surfaces, with messages matching the /privacy page's documented worked example byte-for-byte, and it enforces a real k-anonymity floor on get_aggregated_signal (0 contributions -> percentages:null). BUT under direct adversarial testing (this task's explicit mandate) I found two reproducible breaks of the absolute 'never accepts' promise: (1) a bare numeric date of birth ('01/15/1990' or '1990-01-15', no keyword) was accepted with ZERO adversarial effort across multiple tools/fields, including being echoed verbatim into prepare_consented_card's 'shareable' card output ('Notes: Available starting 01/15/1990 full time') -- confirmed 3 times; a spelled-out date ('born January 15 1990') or a 'DOB:' prefix on the identical numeric date WAS correctly caught, showing the detector leans on a keyword rather than the date pattern for numeric formats. (2) Splitting an SSN's digits across two fields of prepare_consented_card (headline:'SSN part A 123-45', notes:'SSN part B 6789 thanks') was accepted and both fragments were echoed verbatim into that tool's markdown/json 'card' output -- a control check confirmed a full unsplit SSN, and a tightly-packed split with no padding text, were both correctly blocked, so the bypass specifically needs non-trivial text between the two digit-groups. Separately, extensive prompt-injection attempts to elicit a score/ranking/demographic inference all failed structurally (no server-side LLM exists in any tool handler), and the /sources page's legal citations are unusually sophisticated (eCFR ITAR sections, SEAD4/7, and pointedly Mobley v. Workday plus NYC/IL/CO AI-hiring statutes grounding the 'never a score' design in real case law).

engineeringQuality.evidence: 8 sequential MCP calls to explain_rule averaged ~175ms (range 141-238ms); 10 concurrent identical requests all returned HTTP 200 with no errors. Every response carries CSP (default-src 'self'), HSTS (max-age=63072000, preload), X-Frame-Options DENY, X-Content-Type-Options nosniff, and a restrictive Permissions-Policy, on every page and the /mcp endpoint alike. /api/health returned {ok:true, toolCount:14, dataLastVerified:{rules:'2026-11-11', timelines:'2026-11-11'}}. The prepare_signed_attestation round-trip (Ed25519 keypair generated and used entirely locally, server-side signature verification including correct rejection of a tampered payload) demonstrates real, correctly-implemented cryptographic logic, not a rubber stamp. Independently downloaded and read the cited SEAD4 PDF directly (via the Read tool's PDF support) and confirmed its 'Effective: 08 June 2017' date matches the tool's own claim verbatim; spot-checked 20 of the 48 /sources links, 17 resolved cleanly (3 .mil/PACER URLs hit bot-protection that also blocked those domains' bare roots, so inconclusive rather than confirmed-broken). Deducted for: no rate-limiting observed anywhere (a plausible abuse vector, though the one mutating tool, contribute_anonymous_signal, claims its own per-role cooldown that I could not directly test because my own harness's safety classifier blocked that specific write call); and one source cited inline by build_trial_assessment (psychology.iresearchnet.com) that I could not find among the /sources page's advertised complete 48-entry list -- a minor completeness gap.

hardConstraintViolation.detail: (a) PII/CUI accepted/echoed without rejection -- YES, two distinct reproducible findings. First, an unforced one: a bare numeric date of birth ('01/15/1990' or ISO '1990-01-15'), with no keyword nearby, was accepted by the guard across multiple tools/fields with zero adversarial framing, including being echoed verbatim into prepare_consented_card's 'shareable' card markdown/json output ('Notes: Available starting 01/15/1990 full time') -- reproduced 3 times. The identical date spelled out ('born January 15 1990') or prefixed with 'DOB:' WAS correctly caught, showing the detector keys off a keyword rather than the date pattern itself for numeric formats. Second, a deliberately adversarial one: splitting an SSN's digits across two fields of prepare_consented_card (headline='SSN part A 123-45', notes='SSN part B 6789 thanks') was accepted and both fragments were echoed verbatim into that same tool's 'shareable' card output. Control checks confirmed a full unsplit SSN in one field, and a tightly-packed two-field split with no padding text, were both correctly blocked -- so non-trivial text between the digit groups across a field boundary is what defeats the detector. Outside these two confirmed gaps, the guard correctly rejected SSNs (multiple formats), passport numbers, investigation/case numbers, DISS/JPAS/NBIS 'record' text, emails, phone numbers, credit-card numbers, classification markings, image/base64 data, and deeply-nested JSON, every time, across 6+ tools and both the MCP and REST surfaces, matching the /privacy page's documented worked example byte-for-byte. (b) DISS/NBIS/DCSA querying/imitation or screenshot requests -- NO. No tool queries or imitates those systems; every relevant output explicitly states they are FSO-only and never queried by this server; a data:image/png;base64 test was correctly rejected as 'image uploads or screenshots... not accepted.' (c) ITAR-controlled technical data/drawings/specs generated or requested -- NO. build_trial_assessment on a real Anduril 'Flight Test Engineer - Mission Autonomy (UAS - Fury)' posting produced a rubric built only from verbatim-quoted public posting bullets with an explicit itarSafetyNote; no tool generated or solicited technical specs. (d) hire/no-hire score, ranking of people, or demographic inference -- NO. Prompt-injection attempts via free-text fields (explain_rule, get_role_rubric) explicitly asking for a '1-10 suitability score' and an ethnicity guess from a name both failed as plain lookups -- there is no server-side LLM in any tool handler, so generative scoring is structurally impossible, not merely policy-disallowed. verify_evidence on a real GitHub profile (torvalds) returned factual public data only, with an explicit 'never infers... protected characteristics' disclaimer; get_role_rubric/fit_debrief/get_aggregated_signal each explicitly state their output is never a score, ranking, or hire/no-hire read. (e) Unsourced statistic/claim -- essentially NO. Every tool response I inspected carried a sources[] array; I extracted all 48 URLs from the /sources page and independently downloaded and read the cited SEAD4 PDF, confirming its stated effective date matches the tool's claim verbatim. One minor gap: build_trial_assessment inline-cites a source (psychology.iresearchnet.com) I could not find listed among the /sources page's advertised 48 -- a completeness gap in the aggregation, not an unsourced in-context claim. (f) Severe accessibility failure blocking a core task -- NO observed failure, with a caveat: structural signals (skip-link, ARIA tab/switch roles, labeled inputs, focus-visible states) were all present, and I completed a full core-task round trip (open playground, switch tab, type into a labeled field, submit, see the error state, see the recovery button) via automated DOM/keyboard-level interaction without a blocker. I could not verify color-contrast ratios or true screen-reader behavior, since my available tooling exposes DOM structure, not rendered pixels or an actual screen-reader pass.

judges.overallNarrative:
Clearance Lens is, in the parts I could fully verify, an unusually well-engineered and well-sourced product for a niche, genuinely underserved problem. Every one of its 14 tools works end-to-end on the live MCP server and the live REST playground alike, backed by real external data (live a16z speedrun postings, live GitHub API lookups, a real Ed25519 signature round-trip I drove myself with a locally-generated keypair, which the server correctly verified AND correctly rejected once I tampered with it). Its legal/factual grounding is unusually deep for a project this size -- I independently downloaded and read the cited SEAD4 PDF and confirmed its claims verbatim, and the /sources page's 48 citations include not just ITAR/clearance regulations but pointed, specific employment-discrimination case law (Mobley v. Workday) and AI-hiring statutes that visibly inform its 'never a score' design. Structurally, there is no server-side LLM in any tool handler, which makes a hire/no-hire score or demographic inference impossible to elicit by construction, not just policy -- I tried directly via prompt injection and it simply failed as a lookup miss every time.

Where it falls short of its own absolute marketing claims is the PII/CUI guard, which is this product's entire reason for existing. It is broad and well-built -- it caught SSNs, passports, case numbers, clearance-record text, emails, phones, credit cards, classification markings, and even base64 'image' data every single time across six-plus tools and both surfaces. But under the adversarial testing this task asked for, I found it twice: a bare numeric date of birth ('01/15/1990', no keyword) sailed through with zero adversarial effort and landed verbatim in a tool-generated 'shareable' card, and an SSN split across two fields of that same card-builder tool also got through and was echoed back as two labeled fragments. Neither is a wildly exotic attack; the DOB case in particular is just someone typing their birthdate the ordinary way. The same guard subsystem also over-blocks in the other direction, wrongly rejecting a plain, on-topic question about the product's own 'NBIS vs DISS' educational content as if it were a personal record submission -- exactly the kind of mistake that would confuse the non-technical humans the /try playground exists for. I could not get a true pixel-level view of the UI (my tooling reads DOM structure, not rendered screenshots), so my aesthetics judgment rests on strong structural/accessibility evidence (ARIA roles, skip-links, focus rings, a working error-recovery flow I drove via real browser automation) rather than visual polish I can personally vouch for. Taken together: a genuinely capable, thoughtfully sourced product whose core trust promise is strong in breadth but not yet airtight at the edges.
topThreeProblems: The PII/CUI guard misses dates of birth written in ordinary numeric formats (e.g. '01/15/1990' or '1990-01-15') when no keyword like 'DOB' or 'born' is present -- confirmed 3 times across 2 tools, including one case where the date was echoed verbatim into prepare_consented_card's 'shareable' card output. This requires zero adversarial effort; it is simply how a person would normally type a birthdate.

A Social Security Number can be smuggled past the same guard by splitting its digits across two fields of prepare_consented_card (e.g. headline='SSN part A 123-45', notes='SSN part B 6789 thanks') -- both fragments were accepted and echoed verbatim into that tool's markdown/json 'card' output, which the tool's own description calls a shareable artifact for a recruiter. (A full unsplit SSN, and a tightly-packed split with no padding text, were both correctly blocked.)

The same guard over-blocks legitimate, non-personal questions: asking 'what is the difference between NBIS and DISS record systems' via explain_rule is wrongly rejected as submitting personal 'clearance record' text, even though the identical subject answers perfectly when given as the exact topic id ('nbis-diss') -- a real usability trap specifically for the non-agent humans the /try playground is built to serve.
